title: SQL Fundamentals
subtitle: Write accurate SQL queries that filter, join and summarise business data, check them properly, and turn them into paid work or a data role.
description: A practical SQL course built around one small business database, so every query and number can be checked by hand. You move from tables and keys to joins, data checks, CTEs and window functions, then learn to scope, price and protect client work and build a public portfolio.
outcomes: Design simple related tables with primary and foreign keys and load data into a free practice database
Write queries that filter, sort and summarise data with WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING
Combine tables with INNER and LEFT JOIN and detect duplicate-row errors before sharing results
Turn a vague business request into a precise definition and answer it with CTEs and window functions
Scope and price an analysis job and handle client personal data safely
Publish a SQL portfolio project and follow a 90-day plan toward a data opportunity
audience: Women who are comfortable with spreadsheets or basic computing and want practical SQL for reporting, analysis, a data role or freelance work.
tools: A smartphone or laptop with a modern browser
A free SQL tool such as SQLite Fiddle or DB Browser for SQLite
A notes app or text file to save your queries
Optional: a free GitHub or Google account for your portfolio

modules.title: How Databases Think: Tables, Queries and Summaries
modules.overview: You learn how a relational database is organised and write your first real queries: filtering, sorting and summarising. Every example uses one small practice database for a fabric business, so you can check every number yourself.

lessons.title: Inside a relational database: tables, rows, keys and data types
objectives: Describe how a relational database stores data in tables made of rows and columns
Identify the primary key and foreign keys in a set of related tables
Choose a sensible data type for each column in a small business table
Explain why data is split across several tables instead of one big sheet

blocks.text: Almost every app you use, from your bank app to a ride-hailing app to an online shop, keeps its records in a **database**. Most business databases are **relational databases**: the data sits in several **tables**, and the tables are linked to each other through shared ID numbers. **SQL** (Structured Query Language, often said as "sequel" or "S-Q-L") is the language you use to ask those tables questions. It was first developed at IBM in the 1970s and is now an international standard, so the same core commands work in PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle and cloud tools such as Google BigQuery and Supabase.

This course is marked Advanced because it goes past the basics: you will learn joins, data checks, CTEs and window functions, and you will build a portfolio. But we start from the ground so nothing is assumed. Throughout the course we use one practice database for a small fabric business. For example, imagine **Kemi**, who sells Ankara, lace, aso-oke and head ties to customers in several Nigerian cities through WhatsApp, Instagram and a small website.

blocks.name: database-tables
blocks.alt: Linked database tables on a screen
blocks.caption: A relational database is a set of tables that point to each other through shared ID columns.

blocks.text: Tables, rows and columns

A **table** holds one kind of thing: customers, orders or products. Each **column** (also called a field) is one fact about that thing, such as city or order date. Each **row** (also called a record) is one customer or one order. A table looks like a spreadsheet tab, but there are strict rules: every row in a column must hold the same type of value, and every table should have a column that identifies each row uniquely.

head: Table
One row means
Example columns
rows: one order placed by one customer
order_id, customer_id, order_date, channel, status, amount
one product line inside an order

blocks.text: Primary keys and foreign keys

A **primary key** is a column whose value is unique for every row and never empty. In Kemi's database, customer_id is the primary key of customers: Amaka is 1, Bisi is 2, and no other customer can ever be 1. A **foreign key** is a column in one table that holds the primary key of another table. The orders table has a customer_id column, so order 101 with customer_id 1 belongs to Amaka. That single number is the link that later lets you **join** the two tables.

Why not keep everything in one big sheet? Because repeated data goes wrong. If Amaka's city is typed on every one of her orders and she moves from Lagos to Abuja, you must change every row, and if you miss one, your reports disagree with themselves. In a relational design her city lives in exactly one place, the customers table. This idea of storing each fact once is called **normalisation**.

blocks.title: How one order links to its customer
blocks.caption: The foreign key customer_id in orders points back to the primary key in customers, so one customer can have many orders.

blocks.text: Data types you will meet

items: **INTEGER**: whole numbers, such as IDs, quantities, or amounts stored in whole naira.

**DECIMAL or NUMERIC**: exact numbers with decimal places; banks and fintechs use these (or store kobo as integers) for money, never a floating type, because floating types can produce tiny rounding errors.
**TEXT or VARCHAR**: words, names and phone numbers. Phone numbers are text, not numbers, because a leading zero such as 0803 would be lost if stored as a number.
**DATE and TIMESTAMP**: dates and times. Store them in the ISO format YYYY-MM-DD, such as 2026-05-03, so they sort correctly.
**BOOLEAN**: true or false, such as is_active.

blocks.title: Worked example: designing Kemi's tables from her notebook
blocks.context: For example, Kemi has kept orders in a notebook with lines like "3 May, Amaka (Lagos, 0803...), Ankara 6 yards, 18,500 naira, WhatsApp, delivered".
steps: Spot the things (nouns): customer, order, product line. Each becomes a table.
Give each table a primary key: customer_id for customers, order_id for orders.
Move customer details (first_name, city, phone) into customers, once per customer.
In orders, keep only customer_id as a foreign key, plus order_date 2026-05-03, channel WhatsApp, status delivered and amount 18500.
Put each product line in order_items with order_id 101, product Ankara 6 yards, qty 1, unit_price 18500, so one order can hold several products.
blocks.result: Kemi now has 3 linked tables. Amaka's city is stored once, and order 101 can be traced to her through customer_id 1.

blocks.title: Prices in this course
blocks.text: All naira amounts in Kemi's database are made-up practice figures for learning, not real market prices.

Keep this picture in mind for the rest of the course: tables of one kind of thing, a primary key in each, and foreign keys tying them together. Every query you write is simply a question asked of these tables.

takeaways: A relational database stores data in linked tables, each holding one kind of thing.
A primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key points to a primary key in another table.
Store each fact once (normalisation) so reports never disagree.
Pick data types deliberately: phone numbers as text, dates as YYYY-MM-DD, money as exact numbers.

activity.title: Practice task: design a small database on paper
steps: Choose a small business you know, for example a provisions shop or a tailoring business.
List the main things it tracks and turn each into a table name.
For each table write 4 to 6 columns with a data type next to each.
Underline the primary key in each table and draw an arrow from each foreign key to the table it points to.
Write three sample rows for each table using made-up first names.
activity.evidence: A photo of your table design with keys and arrows marked.

lessons.title: Your first queries: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT
objectives: Write a SELECT query that returns chosen columns from one table
Filter rows with WHERE using comparison operators, AND, OR, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and IS NULL
Sort and shorten results with ORDER BY and LIMIT
Explain the order in which the database processes the parts of a query

blocks.text: A query is a polite, precise request: "show me these columns, from this table, for rows that meet this condition, sorted this way". In SQL that sentence becomes four keywords: **SELECT**, **FROM**, **WHERE** and **ORDER BY**. Most everyday questions are answered with only these, plus LIMIT to keep the answer short. Keywords are not case sensitive, but writing them in capitals makes queries easier to read, and most databases expect a semicolon at the end of each statement.
SELECT and FROM

SELECT names the columns you want; FROM names the table. To list every customer's first name and city you write: SELECT first_name, city FROM customers; The star symbol means all columns: SELECT * FROM customers; Use the star only to explore a small table. On real systems with millions of rows it is slow and costly, especially on cloud tools that charge by the amount of data read.

blocks.name: search-results
blocks.alt: A person looking through a list of search results
blocks.caption: A good query returns only the rows and columns that answer the question, nothing more.

blocks.text: Filtering rows with WHERE

WHERE keeps only the rows where a condition is true. Text values go inside single quotes, numbers do not. Dates stored as YYYY-MM-DD text can be compared like text because that format sorts in date order.

head: Operator
Meaning
Example on Kemi's orders
rows: matches any value in a list
within a range, both ends included

blocks.title: Brackets when mixing AND with OR
blocks.text: AND is evaluated before OR. The condition status = 'delivered' AND channel = 'WhatsApp' OR channel = 'Instagram' returns every Instagram order, even cancelled ones. Write status = 'delivered' AND (channel = 'WhatsApp' OR channel = 'Instagram') to say what you mean.
Sorting and limiting

ORDER BY sorts the result. Add DESC for largest first; ASC (smallest first) is the default. You can sort by several columns, such as ORDER BY city, first_name. LIMIT 3 keeps only the first three rows after sorting, which is how you get a top three. LIMIT works in SQLite, MySQL and PostgreSQL; Microsoft SQL Server uses SELECT TOP 3 instead.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's biggest delivered WhatsApp orders
blocks.context: For example, Kemi wants to know which WhatsApp sales were her largest, ignoring cancelled and pending orders. Her orders table has 10 rows.
steps: Write: SELECT order_id, order_date, amount FROM orders
Add the filter: WHERE channel = 'WhatsApp' AND status = 'delivered'
Add the sort: ORDER BY amount DESC;
Check: order 109 is a WhatsApp order but is pending, so it is correctly excluded.
blocks.result: Her largest delivered WhatsApp order was order 105 at 61,000 naira. Adding LIMIT 1 would return only that row.

blocks.text: A second check: SELECT first_name, city FROM customers WHERE phone IS NULL; returns one row, Chioma in Lagos, so Kemi knows whose number to collect. Note that WHERE phone = NULL would return nothing, because NULL means unknown and is never equal to anything. Always use IS NULL.
Removing repeats and matching text

**DISTINCT** removes duplicate rows from the result. SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers; returns each city once: Lagos, Ibadan, Abuja and Port Harcourt, even though Lagos and Abuja each appear on two customers. It is a quick way to see which values a column actually contains before you filter on it, which helps you avoid typing 'lagos' when the data says 'Lagos'.

Text matching rules differ between systems. In PostgreSQL, comparisons with = and LIKE are case sensitive, so use ILIKE for a case-insensitive match. MySQL usually ignores case by default, and SQLite's LIKE ignores case for plain English letters while = does not. When results look too few, check capital letters, extra spaces and spelling in the data first.
The order the database actually works in

You type SELECT first, but the database does not start there. It first finds the table (FROM), throws away rows that fail the condition (WHERE), then picks the columns (SELECT), sorts (ORDER BY) and finally cuts the list (LIMIT). Knowing this explains a common error: in many databases you cannot use a column nickname created in SELECT inside WHERE, because WHERE runs before SELECT.

blocks.title: How a basic query is processed
blocks.caption: The database reads FROM and WHERE before SELECT, which is why filters work on the original columns.

takeaways: SELECT picks columns, FROM picks the table, WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT shortens.
Text and dates go in single quotes; use brackets when mixing AND and OR.
Missing values are NULL and must be tested with IS NULL, never = NULL.
The database runs FROM and WHERE before SELECT.

activity.title: Practice task: answer five questions with simple queries
steps: Using the practice tables from this lesson (you will build them in Module 2, or write on paper for now), write a query for all orders above 20,000 naira.
Write a query for orders placed in June 2026 using BETWEEN.

lessons.title: Summarising data: COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY and HAVING
objectives: Use COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX to summarise a table
Group rows with GROUP BY to produce totals per channel, month or customer
Filter groups with HAVING and explain how it differs from WHERE
Read summary results and check them against a grand total

blocks.text: Managers rarely want a list of 10,000 orders. They want answers such as "how much did we sell last month" or "which channel brings the most money". **Aggregate functions** turn many rows into one number, and **GROUP BY** produces one number per group.

head: Function
What it returns
Note
rows: counts every row, even with NULLs
ignores NULLs, so it divides by non-NULL rows only
works on numbers, text and dates

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's delivered sales in one line
blocks.context: For example, Kemi wants a quick summary of all orders that actually reached customers.
steps: Write: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount), AVG(amount), MIN(amount), MAX(amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered';
The database first keeps the 8 delivered orders out of 10.
Result: 8 orders, total 211,500, average 26,437.5, smallest 8,000, largest 61,000.
Check the average by hand: 211,500 divided by 8 is 26,437.5. Correct.
blocks.result: Delivered revenue is 211,500 naira from 8 orders, about 26,400 naira per order.

blocks.text: GROUP BY: one row per group

Add GROUP BY and the summary is repeated for each value of a column. To see sales by channel: SELECT channel, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY channel ORDER BY revenue DESC; The word AS gives a column a readable name, called an alias.

Always check that groups add back to the total: 101,000 + 83,000 + 27,500 = 211,500, and 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 orders. If the pieces do not add up to the whole, something in your query is wrong. This habit of **reconciling** will save you many times.

blocks.title: The GROUP BY rule
blocks.text: Every column in SELECT must either be inside an aggregate function or listed in GROUP BY. PostgreSQL and SQL Server refuse a query that breaks this rule. SQLite and some MySQL settings accept it but return a value from an arbitrary row, which can quietly give wrong answers. Follow the rule everywhere.
Grouping by month

Dates often need to be cut down to a month first. In SQLite, substr(order_date, 1, 7) turns 2026-05-19 into 2026-05. PostgreSQL uses date_trunc('month', order_date) and MySQL uses DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m'). Kemi's delivered sales by month come out as May 69,500 (3 orders), June 73,500 (2), July 60,500 (2) and August 8,000 (1). Again, 69,500 + 73,500 + 60,500 + 8,000 = 211,500.

blocks.name: bar-chart
blocks.caption: Grouped totals are exactly the numbers you would put in a bar chart for a manager.

blocks.text: How NULLs change your counts

Missing values quietly affect summaries. In Kemi's customers table, SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(phone) FROM customers; returns 6 and 5, because Chioma has no phone recorded and COUNT(phone) skips her. AVG behaves the same way: it divides by the number of non-NULL values, not by the number of rows. If a missing amount should count as zero, say so explicitly with COALESCE(amount, 0), which replaces NULL with 0. Decide which meaning the question needs and write it into the query rather than leaving it to chance.

**COUNT(DISTINCT column)** counts different values. SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered'; returns 5, meaning five different customers received at least one order, even though there were 8 delivered orders. Mixing up orders and customers is one of the most common mistakes in sales reports. Use ROUND(AVG(amount), 0) when you want a tidy whole-naira average for a manager.
WHERE versus HAVING

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. **HAVING** filters whole groups after the totals are calculated, so it can test an aggregate. To find repeat buyers: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS spent FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2; The answer is customer 1 (3 orders, 55,000) and customer 2 (2 orders, 54,500). In the next module you will join these IDs to names: they are Amaka and Bisi.

blocks.title: WHERE or HAVING?
blocks.caption: Use WHERE for conditions on single rows and HAVING for conditions on group totals.

blocks.text: The full processing order is now FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Writing the clauses in that logical order in your head is the fastest way to understand why a query behaves the way it does. When a summary looks strange, rebuild it one clause at a time: run FROM and WHERE alone, check the row count, then add GROUP BY, then HAVING.

takeaways: Aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) turn many rows into one value.
GROUP BY gives one summary row per group; every non-aggregated column must be in GROUP BY.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.
Reconcile: group totals must add back to the grand total.

quiz.q: In Kemi's database, orders has a column customer_id that holds values from customers.customer_id. What is orders.customer_id?
quiz.explain: It points to the primary key of another table, which makes it a foreign key. It allows orders to be linked to customers.

quiz.q: Why should a customer phone number like 08031234567 be stored as TEXT rather than INTEGER?
options: Text uses less storage in every database
An integer would drop the leading zero
SQL does not allow integers over 1,000
quiz.explain: Stored as a number, 0803... becomes 803..., losing the leading zero. Phone numbers are labels, not quantities.

quiz.q: Which query correctly finds customers with no phone number recorded?
options: SELECT first_name FROM customers WHERE phone = NULL;
SELECT first_name FROM customers WHERE phone = '';
SELECT first_name FROM customers WHERE phone IS NOT NULL;
SELECT first_name FROM customers WHERE phone IS NULL;
quiz.explain: NULL is never equal to anything, so = NULL returns no rows. IS NULL is the correct test.

quiz.q: Delivered sales by channel are WhatsApp 101,000, Instagram 83,000 and Website 27,500, but the overall delivered total query returns 211,500. What does this tell you?
options: The groups reconcile, so the channel query is consistent
quiz.explain: 101,000 + 83,000 + 27,500 = 211,500, so the groups add back to the total, which is the check you want.

quiz.q: A colleague writes SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE SUM(amount) > 50000 GROUP BY customer_id; and gets an error. What should she change?
options: Move the condition into HAVING SUM(amount) > 50000 after GROUP BY
Put the condition in ORDER BY
quiz.explain: WHERE runs before grouping and cannot use aggregates. A condition on a group total belongs in HAVING.

quiz.q: Which list shows the order in which the database processes these clauses?
quiz.explain: The table is found first, rows are filtered, columns are chosen, and only then is the result sorted.

modules.title: Tools, Joins and Trustworthy Results
modules.overview: You set up a free practice database, combine tables with joins, and learn the checks that separate a believable number from a correct one. By the end you can build a multi-table report and prove it adds up.

objectives: Choose a free SQL practice tool that suits your phone, laptop and data budget
Create tables with CREATE TABLE, including primary and foreign keys
Load rows with INSERT and confirm them with a row count
Save and back up your practice work so it is not lost

blocks.text: You learn SQL by typing queries and seeing results, so you need somewhere to run them. You do not need to buy anything or install a server. The options below are free, and they run the same core SQL you met in Module 1. Choose one and stay with it for this course; you can learn the others later.

Where it runs
Good for
Watch out for

Instant practice, no account, no install
Data lives in the browser tab; copy your queries out to save them

blocks.name: typing-code
blocks.alt: A person typing code on a laptop
blocks.caption: Practice means typing real queries and checking the results, not only reading about them.

blocks.title: Saving data on a phone
blocks.text: SQLite Fiddle and DB Browser for SQLite run on your own device after loading, so practising does not use data for every query. Write your queries in a notes app or a text file as you go, then paste them in. That file becomes your query library.
Creating a table

CREATE TABLE defines a table's name, its columns and their types. PRIMARY KEY marks the unique ID column. REFERENCES marks a foreign key and tells the database which table it points to. NOT NULL forbids empty values in a column that must always be filled.

items: CREATE TABLE customers (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, first_name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT, phone TEXT, joined_on TEXT);
CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(customer_id), order_date TEXT, channel TEXT, status TEXT, amount INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id INTEGER REFERENCES orders(order_id), product TEXT, qty INTEGER, unit_price INTEGER);

blocks.text: SQLite stores dates as text, which is why order_date is TEXT here. PostgreSQL and MySQL have a proper DATE type, and you should use it there. Amounts are stored as whole naira in INTEGER for simplicity; a real payments system would store exact decimals or the amount in kobo.
Adding rows with INSERT

INSERT INTO adds rows. You can add many rows in one statement by separating them with commas: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Amaka', 'Lagos', '0803xxx0001', '2025-11-02'), (2, 'Bisi', 'Ibadan', '0805xxx0002', '2025-12-15'); and so on. Text goes in single quotes and NULL (without quotes) means the value is missing, as for Chioma's phone. A name with an apostrophe, such as Ngozi's, is written with two single quotes inside the text: 'Ngozi''s'.

blocks.title: Worked example: loading Kemi's practice database and checking it
blocks.context: For example, Ada is starting this course on her phone during lunch breaks and uses SQLite Fiddle in her browser.
steps: She opens sqlite.org/fiddle and pastes the three CREATE TABLE statements, then runs them.
She pastes INSERT statements for 6 customers, 10 orders and 13 order_items rows, copied from the course table in her notes app.
She checks: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers; returns 6. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; returns 10. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items; returns 13.
She checks totals: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders; returns 251,500 for all 10 orders, matching the figure she expected.
She saves the whole script in her notes app titled kemi_setup.sql so she can rebuild the database any time.
blocks.result: Ada has a working database in under 15 minutes. The row counts (6, 10, 13) and the total (251,500) prove the load is complete.

blocks.text: Why check counts and totals straight after loading? Because a missing comma or quote can stop one INSERT while others succeed. If you skip the check, every later answer is wrong and you will not know why. Professionals do the same when they import a CSV export from a sales app: count the rows in the file, count the rows in the table, and compare.
Importing a spreadsheet

Most real data arrives as a spreadsheet. Save the sheet as CSV (comma separated values), with one header row and no merged cells, totals rows or blank rows. DB Browser for SQLite has File, Import, Table from CSV file. Before importing, make dates YYYY-MM-DD, remove naira signs and thousand separators from amounts, and keep phone numbers as text so the leading zero survives.

blocks.title: Before you trust a new practice database
blocks.caption: Run these five checks every time you build or import a database.

blocks.title: Practice data only
blocks.text: Never paste real customer names, phone numbers or account details into a public online tool. Use made-up or anonymised data for practice. Real client data has rules, covered in Module 3.

takeaways: Free tools such as SQLite Fiddle, DB Browser for SQLite, a free PostgreSQL project or the BigQuery sandbox are enough to learn.
CREATE TABLE defines columns, types, primary and foreign keys; INSERT adds rows.
Check row counts and totals straight after loading data.
Keep your setup script in a file so you can rebuild the database any time.

lessons.title: Joining tables: INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and a question-to-answer workflow
objectives: Combine two tables with INNER JOIN on a shared key
Use LEFT JOIN to keep rows that have no match, such as customers with no orders
Use table aliases to keep join queries short and clear
Follow a five-step workflow from business question to checked answer

blocks.text: Because a relational database stores each fact once, most useful questions need data from more than one table. "Which city brings Kemi the most money?" needs city from customers and amount from orders. A **JOIN** lines up rows from two tables wherever the key values match.
INNER JOIN: only the matches

SELECT c.first_name, c.city, o.order_id, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered'; The letters o and c are **table aliases**, short names you give each table so you can write c.city instead of customers.city. ON states how rows match. JOIN on its own means INNER JOIN: a row appears only when there is a match on both sides. This query returns 8 rows, one per delivered order, each now carrying the customer's name and city.

blocks.name: data-processing
blocks.caption: A join brings matching rows from two tables together into one result.

blocks.text: LEFT JOIN: keep everyone on the left

LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the first (left) table, even when the right table has no match; the missing columns come back as NULL. This is how you find who is missing. Kemi's customers table has 6 people, but only 5 have delivered orders.

blocks.title: Worked example: total spend per customer, including those who have not bought
blocks.context: For example, Kemi wants a list of all 6 customers with their delivered spend, so she can send a special offer to anyone who has not bought yet.
steps: Start from customers so nobody is lost: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
Summarise per customer: SELECT c.first_name, COUNT(o.order_id) AS orders, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS spent ... GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY spent DESC;
Result: Dupe 1 order 61,000; Amaka 3 orders 55,000; Bisi 2 orders 54,500; Efe 1 order 33,000; Chioma 1 order 8,000; Funmi 0 orders 0.
Check: 61,000 + 55,000 + 54,500 + 33,000 + 8,000 + 0 = 211,500, the delivered total from Module 1.
blocks.result: Funmi has never received an order, so she is the target for the welcome offer. The totals reconcile to 211,500.

blocks.title: Where you put the filter matters
blocks.text: In the example, status = 'delivered' sits inside the ON clause. If you move it to WHERE, Funmi's row (where status is NULL) is filtered out and your LEFT JOIN silently behaves like an INNER JOIN. Conditions on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN usually belong in ON.

COUNT(o.order_id) counts only real matches, so Funmi gets 0. COUNT(*) would have given her 1, because the LEFT JOIN still produces one row for her, filled with NULLs. This small difference changes reports.

blocks.title: INNER JOIN versus LEFT JOIN
blocks.caption: Use INNER JOIN when you only want matched pairs and LEFT JOIN when you must keep every row of the main table.

blocks.text: Joining and grouping together

Joins and GROUP BY combine naturally. Revenue by city: SELECT c.city, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY c.city ORDER BY revenue DESC; gives Lagos 63,000, Abuja 61,000, Ibadan 54,500 and Port Harcourt 33,000. Lagos is top only because it has two buyers, Amaka and Chioma; Abuja's 61,000 comes from one order by Dupe. That insight is worth saying out loud in a report.

You can chain joins to reach a third table. To see which products each customer bought: FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id. Each JOIN needs its own ON condition. Always join on the key columns, never on names or cities: two customers can share the first name Amaka, but they can never share a customer_id. A missing or wrong ON condition pairs every row with every row and produces a huge, meaningless result.

Other join types exist. RIGHT JOIN is a LEFT JOIN written the other way round, FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides, and CROSS JOIN pairs every row with every row. In daily analysis, INNER and LEFT cover most needs.
A workflow from question to answer

items: Write the question in one sentence with a time period and a definition, for example: delivered revenue per city, May to August 2026.
Explore the tables: list columns, run SELECT * ... LIMIT 5, and check which keys link them.
Build the query in small pieces: run the FROM and JOIN first, check the row count, then add WHERE, then GROUP BY.
Verify: reconcile to a known total and spot-check two rows by hand.
Present the answer in plain words with the number, the period and any caveat.

takeaways: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match on both sides.
LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the first table and fills missing matches with NULL.
Put conditions on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN in the ON clause.
Build join queries step by step and reconcile the result to a known total.

activity.title: Practice task: answer three join questions
steps: Write an INNER JOIN listing every delivered order with the customer's first name and city.
Write a LEFT JOIN that lists all customers with their number of delivered orders, including zero.
Write a query for delivered revenue per city and check it adds to 211,500.
For each query, write one sentence that answers the business question in plain words.
activity.evidence: Your three queries, their results and the three plain-word answers in one document.

lessons.title: Checking your work: duplicate rows, NULLs, CASE and readable queries
objectives: Detect and fix row duplication caused by one-to-many joins
Handle NULLs and integer division correctly in calculations
Group values into categories with CASE
Format and comment queries so others can review them

blocks.text: A query that runs without an error is not necessarily right. The dangerous mistakes are the silent ones: the query runs, the number looks believable, and a manager makes a decision on it. This lesson covers the checks professionals use before they share a number.
The duplicate-row trap

When you join a table to another that has several matching rows for each key, the first table's rows are repeated. One order with two product lines becomes two rows after joining to order_items. If you then add up the order amount, that order is counted twice. This is called **fan-out**, and it is the most common cause of inflated totals.

blocks.title: Worked example: why revenue suddenly jumped
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi is helping Kemi and wants revenue with product details, so she joins orders to order_items.
steps: She runs: SELECT SUM(o.amount) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered'; The answer is 293,500.
She compares with the known delivered total from orders alone: 211,500. The difference is 82,000.
She counts rows after the join: 11 rows, not 8. Orders 102, 106 and 108 each have two product lines, so each appears twice.
She checks the gap: 42,000 + 12,500 + 27,500 = 82,000. That is exactly the three duplicated amounts.
Fix: sum at the right level. For product revenue use SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) from order_items; for order revenue sum orders.amount without joining items.
blocks.result: The correct delivered revenue is 211,500. The 293,500 figure overstated it by 82,000 because of fan-out.

blocks.title: A quick fan-out test
blocks.text: Before and after adding a join, run SELECT COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT order_id). If the first grows but the second does not, rows are being repeated and any SUM of order-level columns will be wrong.
NULLs and arithmetic

items: Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 5000 + NULL is NULL. Use COALESCE(column, 0) when a missing value really means zero.
AVG ignores NULLs, so the average is over rows that have a value. Decide whether that is what the question means.
Integer division: in SQLite, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, 7 / 2 returns 3 when both numbers are integers. Write 7 * 1.0 / 2 or CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2 to get 3.5. MySQL returns 3.5000 either way.
Percentages: share of WhatsApp revenue is 101000 * 100.0 / 211500, which is about 47.8 percent. Without the .0 some databases return 47.

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person checking data on a large screen
blocks.caption: Checking a number before sharing it is part of the job, not an extra.

blocks.text: Grouping values with CASE

CASE works like an if-then rule inside a query. It lets you create categories that do not exist in the data. For example: SELECT CASE WHEN amount >= 30000 THEN 'large' WHEN amount >= 15000 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'small' END AS size, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY size;

Check: 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 orders and 136,000 + 46,000 + 29,500 = 211,500. CASE checks conditions from top to bottom and stops at the first true one, so put the most specific or highest threshold first. Always include ELSE, or unmatched rows become NULL.
Make queries readable

items: Put each clause (SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY) on its own line.
Use clear aliases such as c for customers and o for orders, and name result columns with AS.
Add a comment line starting with two hyphens at the top: the question, the date and your name. Everything after -- on that line is ignored by the database.
Never use SELECT * in a query you hand over; list the columns so readers know what they get.

blocks.title: Before you share a number
blocks.caption: Five quick checks that catch most silent errors in SQL reports.

blocks.text: Where possible, reconcile with a source outside the database too. If Kemi's payment provider dashboard shows 211,500 naira received for delivered orders in the same period, your SQL total is confirmed by an independent record. If the two differ, list the orders that explain the gap, such as an order paid in cash on delivery or a refund, before reporting either number. Write the explanation down so the next report starts from the same understanding.
Finally, be honest about limits. If 15 percent of orders have no channel recorded, say so beside the channel chart. A clear caveat protects the decision and your reputation.

takeaways: Joining to a many-rows table repeats rows (fan-out) and inflates sums.
Compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT key) to detect fan-out.
Handle NULLs with COALESCE and avoid integer division by multiplying by 1.0.
CASE builds categories; always include ELSE and reconcile the groups.
Format and comment queries so someone else can check them.

activity.title: Practice task: audit a wrong query
steps: Run the join of orders to order_items and sum orders.amount; note the inflated result.
Run COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) on the same join and explain the difference.
Rewrite the query to give product revenue correctly using qty times unit_price.
Write a CASE query that sorts delivered orders into your own three size bands and reconcile the totals.
Format your final queries with one clause per line and a comment header.
activity.evidence: Your before and after queries with a short note explaining the error and the fix.

quiz.q: Ada loads Kemi's data and SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders returns 9, but the source has 10 orders. What should she do first?
options: Carry on, one row will not matter
Find which INSERT failed and reload before running any analysis
Delete all tables and switch tools
quiz.explain: A count mismatch means the load is incomplete, so every later result would be wrong. Fix the load first.

quiz.q: Which query lists all 6 customers with their delivered order count, including customers with none?
options: customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered'
orders o INNER JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
quiz.explain: Only the LEFT JOIN with the status condition inside ON keeps customers who have no delivered orders. Putting it in WHERE removes them.

quiz.q: Joining orders to order_items raised delivered revenue from 211,500 to 293,500. What is the most likely cause?
options: Orders with several product lines were counted more than once
quiz.explain: This is fan-out: orders 102, 106 and 108 have two item rows each, so their amounts (82,000 in total) were added twice.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, SELECT 3 / 4; returns 0. How should you calculate 0.75?
quiz.explain: Make one value a decimal before dividing. 3 / 4 * 1.0 still divides integers first and gives 0.

quiz.q: A CASE expression has WHEN amount >= 15000 THEN 'medium' listed before WHEN amount >= 30000 THEN 'large'. What happens to a 61,000 order?
options: It is labelled medium, because CASE stops at the first true condition
quiz.explain: CASE checks conditions in order. 61,000 is at least 15,000, so it stops at 'medium'. Put the highest threshold first.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest reason to put status = 'delivered' in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN rather than in WHERE?
options: It makes the query run faster in every database
It keeps left-table rows that have no delivered match
ON is required for every filter
quiz.explain: A WHERE test on the right-hand table removes the NULL rows, turning the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.

modules.title: Analysis Projects, Clients and Your Portfolio
modules.overview: You learn to turn vague requests into precise questions, write multi-step analyses with CTEs and window functions, price and scope paid work, protect client data, and build a public portfolio with a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: From vague request to precise query: discovery questions, subqueries and CTEs
objectives: Ask discovery questions that turn a vague data request into a precise, answerable question
Write a subquery that compares each row with an overall figure
Break a multi-step analysis into readable steps with a CTE (WITH clause)
Confirm definitions with the requester before running the final query

blocks.text: Requests rarely arrive as clean questions. A manager says "send me our best customers" or "how are sales doing". If you start typing SQL straight away, you will answer your own guess, not her question. The first skill of a data professional is **discovery**: a short conversation that pins down exactly what is wanted and why.
Discovery questions to ask every time

head: Ask
Why it matters
Example answer for Kemi
rows: Choose who gets a loyalty discount
How do you define the key word (best, active, sale)?
Highest delivered spend, not number of orders
Cancelled, test or refunded records distort results
A number, a list or a chart need different work
A short list with names, by Friday
Recurring work should be saved and reusable

blocks.name: questions
blocks.alt: A person surrounded by question marks
blocks.caption: Good questions before the query save hours of rework after it.

blocks.text: Write the agreed definition back in one sentence and get a yes: "Best customers means customers whose delivered spend from May to August 2026 is above the average delivered spend per buying customer." Now the query is almost obvious, and nobody can later say you answered the wrong question.

blocks.title: From request to answer
blocks.caption: Discovery turns a loose request into a definition you can query and defend.

blocks.text: Subqueries: a query inside a query

To compare each row with an overall figure, you can place one query inside another, in brackets. For example: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' AND amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered'); The inner query works out the average order, 26,437.5, and the outer query returns the orders above it: 102 (42,000), 105 (61,000), 107 (33,000) and 108 (27,500). Subqueries can also follow IN, such as WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE channel = 'Instagram').

A subquery placed in WHERE must return the right shape. After a comparison such as > it must return exactly one value; after IN it may return a list of values from one column. If a subquery that should return one value returns several, the database raises an error, which is a helpful warning that your inner logic is not what you thought.
CTEs: name each step

When an analysis has several steps, nested brackets become hard to read. A **CTE** (common table expression) lets you name a step with WITH, then use it like a table. CTEs work in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite, BigQuery and MySQL 8.0 and later.

blocks.title: Worked example: Kemi's best customers by the agreed definition
blocks.context: For example, Kemi agreed that best customers are those with delivered spend from May to August 2026 above the average spend per buying customer.
steps: Step 1, name the totals: WITH spend AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' AND order_date BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-08-31' GROUP BY customer_id)
Step 2, check the step alone: it returns 5 customers with totals 55,000, 54,500, 8,000, 61,000 and 33,000, which add to 211,500.
Step 3, the average per buying customer is 211,500 divided by 5 = 42,300.
Step 4, the final query: SELECT c.first_name, s.total FROM spend s JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id WHERE s.total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM spend) ORDER BY s.total DESC;
Result: Dupe 61,000, Amaka 55,000 and Bisi 54,500.
blocks.result: Three customers qualify. Kemi can see that Dupe made one large purchase while Amaka bought three times, which may change who gets which offer.

blocks.title: Say what the number hides
blocks.text: The definition was spend, so Amaka (3 orders) and Dupe (1 order) look alike. Mention it. A good analyst answers the question asked and points out what the requester may want to know next.
A second common request: lapsed customers

"Who has gone quiet?" needs a definition too, for example customers whose last delivered order was before 1 July 2026, or who have never received one. SELECT c.first_name, MAX(o.order_date) AS last_order FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name HAVING MAX(o.order_date) IS NULL OR MAX(o.order_date) < '2026-07-01'; returns Bisi (last order 2026-06-21), Dupe (2026-06-10) and Funmi (no order). Notice that Dupe is both a best customer and a lapsed one, which is a useful finding for Kemi's WhatsApp follow-up list.

takeaways: Discovery questions turn vague requests into definitions you can query.
Write the definition back in one sentence and get agreement before the final query.
Subqueries compare rows with overall figures; CTEs name each step for readability.
Check each CTE step on its own before building on it.

activity.title: Practice task: run a discovery conversation
steps: Ask a friend or colleague with a small business what they would like to know from their sales records.
Use the six discovery questions and write down the answers.
Write the agreed definition in one sentence and read it back to them.
Write a CTE query that would answer it on Kemi's practice database or your own data.
Record the result and one extra point the requester may want to know.
activity.evidence: Your discovery notes, the one-sentence definition and the CTE query with its result.

lessons.title: Scoping, pricing and handling client data safely
objectives: Write a scope that lists the exact questions, data period and deliverables
Estimate the hours for an analysis job and turn them into a quote
Control scope changes politely without losing the client
Apply basic data protection practice when working with client data in Nigeria

blocks.text: Once you can write reliable queries, people will ask you to do it for them: an employer, a business owner, an NGO or a fintech startup. Whether you are paid a salary or a project fee, the same discipline applies: agree what will be delivered, estimate the work honestly, and protect the data you are trusted with.
What a good scope contains

items: **The questions**, numbered and written as agreed definitions, for example: Q1 delivered revenue per month, May to August 2026.
**The data**: which system or export, which tables, which period, and who gives you access.
**The deliverables**: a short report, a spreadsheet of results, the saved SQL file, or a dashboard.
**Review rounds**: for example one round of corrections included.
**Exclusions**: what is not included, such as cleaning data from a second system or building automated reports.
**Timeline and payment terms**: delivery date, deposit and balance.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A person reviewing and signing a contract
blocks.caption: A written scope protects both you and the client from misunderstandings.

blocks.text: Estimating time honestly

Beginners often price only the time to type the final query. In real work, understanding unfamiliar tables, chasing access, cleaning odd values and checking results usually take longer than the query itself. Estimate each stage, add a buffer for surprises, then multiply by your hourly rate. Your rate depends on your experience, the client and the market, so research it yourself; the figure below is only for the arithmetic.

blocks.title: Worked example: quoting a sales analysis for a boutique
blocks.context: For example, Halima is asked by a Kaduna boutique owner to answer four questions from a sales export: revenue by month, by channel, top 10 customers and repeat purchase rate. She uses an illustrative rate of 5,000 naira per hour; this is not a market rate, only a number to show the method.
steps: Discovery call and written scope: 2 hours.
Getting access, loading the export and checking row counts: 3 hours.
Writing and testing four queries: 5 hours.
Reconciliation and spot checks: 2 hours.
Short report with charts and plain-language findings: 3 hours.
Subtotal 15 hours. Buffer of 20 percent: 15 x 0.2 = 3 hours. Total 18 hours.
Quote: 18 x 5,000 = 90,000 naira, with 50 percent (45,000) as a deposit before access is granted.
blocks.result: Halima quotes 90,000 naira for four defined questions with one review round, and the scope says extra questions are priced separately.

blocks.text: Send the scope in writing, even if the client is a friend, and ask for a short reply such as "Agreed". A WhatsApp message is better than nothing, but a one-page document or email is easier to refer back to. If the client's data turns out to be much messier than expected, tell them early, explain what extra work is needed, and agree any change in price before doing it, not after.
Handling extra requests

Analysis invites curiosity: "while you are there, can you also check...". Small additions add up. A calm, friendly reply works: "Happy to. That is a new question outside our four, so I will send a small add-on quote, about 3 hours." Keep a numbered list of requests so both of you can see what was agreed and what was added.

blocks.title: Life of a paid analysis job
blocks.caption: Each stage has a clear output, and the job ends with handing over files and removing the client's data.

blocks.text: Protecting client data

Sales and customer data usually contain **personal data**: names, phone numbers, addresses and purchase history. In Nigeria, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for processing personal data, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) oversees it. You do not need to be a lawyer to follow good practice, but you should know the law exists and ask the client how they meet it.

blocks.title: Safe data habits for analysts
blocks.text: Ask for read-only access, so you cannot change or delete records by mistake. Request only the columns you need; you rarely need phone numbers to count sales. Replace names with IDs in anything you share. Never send exports through personal WhatsApp chats or groups, and never paste real customer data into public online tools. Store files in a password-protected account with two-step verification, and delete them at the end of the job, then confirm the deletion in writing.

Read-only access also protects you from the most damaging SQL commands. DELETE, UPDATE and DROP change or remove data, and on many systems there is no undo. If you ever must run one, first run the same WHERE condition in a SELECT to see exactly which rows would be affected, and make sure a backup exists.

takeaways: A scope lists the questions as definitions, the data, deliverables, review rounds, exclusions and payment.
Estimate every stage plus a buffer; the final query is a small part of the time.
Handle extra requests with a friendly add-on quote and a numbered request list.
Protect personal data: read-only access, minimum columns, no WhatsApp sharing, delete at the end.

activity.title: Practice task: write a one-page scope and quote
steps: Choose a realistic small analysis job with three to five questions.
Write each question as an agreed definition with a period.
Estimate hours for each stage, add a 20 percent buffer and calculate the quote with a rate you have researched.
Add a data-handling paragraph covering access, minimum columns, storage and deletion.
Ask someone to read it and tell you anything that is unclear.
activity.evidence: Your one-page scope with the hours table and the data-handling paragraph.

lessons.title: Window functions, a public portfolio and your 90-day plan
objectives: Use ROW_NUMBER, running SUM and LAG window functions to analyse trends
Choose a public dataset and plan a portfolio analysis from question to verified answer
Publish queries with a clear README that explains the business question
Write a 90-day plan toward a specific SQL-related opportunity

blocks.text: Window functions are where many learners move from basic to confident SQL. They calculate across a set of rows while keeping every row, unlike GROUP BY which collapses rows into one. They work in PostgreSQL, SQL Server, BigQuery, SQLite 3.25 and later, and MySQL 8.0 and later.
Three window functions worth knowing

head: Function
What it does
Typical question
rows: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)
Which was each customer's first order?
How much have we sold so far this year?
How did this month compare with last month?

blocks.text: PARTITION BY restarts the calculation for each group, like a GROUP BY that does not collapse rows. ORDER BY inside OVER sets the order the window moves through. In Kemi's data, ROW_NUMBER partitioned by customer shows Amaka's orders as 1 (101), 2 (103) and 3 (108). Filtering to row number 1 gives each customer's first order, which is how analysts measure new customers per month.

blocks.title: Worked example: monthly revenue, running total and change
blocks.context: For example, Kemi wants one table showing each month's delivered revenue, the running total and the change from the previous month.
steps: Step 1, a CTE for monthly revenue: WITH m AS (SELECT substr(order_date, 1, 7) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY month)
Step 2: SELECT month, revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS running_total, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change FROM m;
Result for 2026-05: revenue 69,500, running total 69,500, change empty (NULL, as there is no earlier month).
2026-08: 8,000, running total 211,500, change -52,500. Check: the final running total equals the delivered total.
blocks.result: Revenue peaked in June. August looks like a sharp fall, but the practice data has only one August order, so the honest note is that August may be incomplete.

blocks.name: portfolio-website
blocks.alt: A portfolio website shown on a screen
blocks.caption: A public portfolio lets employers and clients see your queries and how you think.

blocks.text: Building a portfolio that proves skill

Certificates say you studied; a portfolio shows you can do the work. Choose one public dataset that connects to a business question you care about. Kaggle hosts many free datasets, including retail and sales data, and the World Bank Open Data site offers country indicators for Nigeria and other African countries. Load it into your practice tool, then work through the same workflow from this course.

items: Write 3 to 5 business questions as clear definitions.
Write one query per question, from simple filtering to joins, aggregates, a CTE and a window function.
Record the checks you ran: row counts, reconciliations and spot checks.
Write findings in plain language with one or two charts made in Google Sheets, Excel or Looker Studio.
Publish the .sql files and a README on GitHub, or a Google Doc with a share link, and pin it to your LinkedIn profile.

blocks.title: What a good README says
blocks.text: For each query: the business question, the definition you used, the query, the result table, and one sentence on what it means. Add a short note on data limits. Reviewers read the explanations as closely as the code.
Good portfolio questions

Strong portfolio questions sound like what a manager would ask: which product category grew fastest over the period, which customers bought once and never returned, what share of revenue comes from the top 10 percent of customers. Weak questions only show syntax, such as "list all rows where price is above 100". Each query should end with a sentence that a non-technical reader could act on, and at least one should show a check you ran and what it caught.
Your 90-day plan

Name one target: for example a junior data analyst role at a fintech or startup, a data support role at an NGO, or freelance reporting for small businesses. Read five real job adverts or client requests for that target and list the skills that keep repeating. SQL often appears beside spreadsheets, a dashboard tool such as Power BI, Tableau or Looker Studio, and clear writing.

blocks.title: A 90-day SQL plan
blocks.caption: Practice first, then prove it publicly, then put it in front of the people who hire.

blocks.text: Make each phase measurable: for example 30 practice queries in month one, one finished project with a README in month two, and ten tailored applications or pitches in the last month. Review your plan every Friday and adjust it.

takeaways: Window functions calculate across rows without collapsing them: ROW_NUMBER, running SUM and LAG.
PARTITION BY restarts the calculation per group; ORDER BY inside OVER sets the direction.
A portfolio shows questions, queries, checks and plain-language findings.
A 90-day plan names one target and sets measurable weekly actions.

activity.title: Practice task: start your portfolio
steps: Run the monthly running total and LAG query on Kemi's practice data and confirm the figures.
Choose one public dataset and write three business questions about it.
Create a GitHub repository or shared document with a README template.
Write your 90-day plan with one target and measurable actions for each month.
activity.evidence: The link to your portfolio repository or document, and your written 90-day plan.

quiz.q: A manager asks for 'our most active customers'. What should the analyst do before writing the final query?
options: Use number of orders, since that is the usual meaning
Ask how 'active' is defined, for which period and what decision it supports, then confirm in writing
Send all customers sorted by name
Use total spend because it is easier
quiz.explain: 'Active' can mean many things. Agreeing the definition and period first prevents answering the wrong question.

quiz.q: In Kemi's data, five customers have delivered spend totalling 211,500. A CTE finds customers above the average per buying customer. What is that average?
quiz.explain: 211,500 divided by 5 buying customers is 42,300. 26,437.5 is the average per order, a different figure.

quiz.q: Halima estimates 12 hours of work and adds a 25 percent buffer, at an illustrative rate of 4,000 naira per hour. What is her quote?
quiz.explain: 12 hours plus 25 percent is 15 hours, and 15 x 4,000 = 60,000 naira.

quiz.q: A client sends a full customer export, including phone numbers, to Halima's personal WhatsApp. She only needs sales totals. What is the best response?
options: Forward it to her study group for help
Keep it in her chat for future jobs
Ask for a version with only the columns she needs through a secure channel, and delete the WhatsApp copy
Post a sample online to ask how to clean it
quiz.explain: Good practice is minimum data, secure storage and deletion. Phone numbers are personal data she does not need.

quiz.q: Monthly revenue is 69,500 in May and 73,500 in June. What does revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) return for June?
quiz.explain: LAG gives the previous month's value, 69,500. 73,500 - 69,500 = 4,000. NULL appears only for the first month.

quiz.q: Before running DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled'; on a client database, what should an analyst do first?
options: Run SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled'; to see the affected rows and confirm a backup exists
Run it twice to be sure
Remove the WHERE clause to keep it simple
Nothing, DELETE can always be undone
quiz.explain: Preview the exact rows with the same WHERE condition and make sure a backup exists. On many systems a DELETE cannot be undone.

finalQuiz.q: Which column should be the primary key of a customers table?
finalQuiz.explain: customer_id is unique for every customer and never empty. Names and cities repeat, and phones can be missing or change.

finalQuiz.q: Which WHERE clause returns delivered orders from either WhatsApp or Instagram only?
finalQuiz.explain: IN keeps the two channels together, so the delivered condition applies to both. Without brackets, AND binds before OR.

finalQuiz.q: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(phone) FROM customers; returns 6 and 5. What does that tell you?
options: One customer has no phone recorded
finalQuiz.explain: COUNT(column) skips NULLs, so one of the 6 customers has a missing phone.

finalQuiz.q: Delivered orders total 211,500 across 8 orders. What is the average order value?
Which clause filters groups after totals are calculated?
finalQuiz.explain: HAVING runs after GROUP BY, so it can test aggregates such as SUM or COUNT.

finalQuiz.q: After loading a CSV, what is the quickest proof that the import is complete?
options: The first five rows look right
Row counts and totals match the source file
The table has the right name
finalQuiz.explain: Matching row counts and totals against the source catches missing or partly loaded rows.

finalQuiz.q: Kemi has 6 customers and Funmi has never ordered. Which join lists all 6 with their order counts?
options: INNER JOIN from orders to customers
LEFT JOIN from customers to orders
INNER JOIN from customers to orders
finalQuiz.explain: A LEFT JOIN starting from customers keeps every customer, and Funmi's order columns come back NULL.

finalQuiz.q: A report shows revenue 30 percent higher after a join to an order_items table was added. What should you check first?
options: Whether the join repeats order rows (fan-out)
Whether the table names are capitalised
finalQuiz.explain: Joining to a many-rows table repeats each order once per item, so summing order amounts double counts.

finalQuiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what does SELECT 9 / 2; return?
finalQuiz.explain: Both values are integers, so integer division returns 4. Write 9 * 1.0 / 2 to get 4.5.

finalQuiz.q: A requester says 'send me the best customers'. What is the most professional next step?
options: Agree a written definition, period and purpose first
finalQuiz.explain: Discovery turns a vague word like 'best' into a definition you can query and defend.

finalQuiz.q: Which window function gives the value from the previous month's row?
finalQuiz.explain: LAG returns the value from the previous row in the window order, so revenue - LAG(revenue) gives the change.

finalQuiz.q: Which habit best protects client personal data during an analysis job?
options: Keep a copy of every export for future work
Share exports in a WhatsApp group for quick feedback
Use read-only access, request only needed columns and delete files at the end
Paste the data into a public online tool to clean it
finalQuiz.explain: Minimum data, read-only access, secure storage and deletion are core good practice under data protection rules.

capstone.title: SQL Query Portfolio Project
capstone.brief: Produce a public portfolio project: a set of queries of increasing difficulty on a real or public dataset, each tied to a business question, plus a documented end-to-end analysis and a 90-day plan toward a named SQL opportunity.
steps: Choose a public dataset (for example from Kaggle or World Bank Open Data) or anonymised data you have permission to use, and load it into your practice tool with row-count checks.
Write 5 business questions as one-sentence definitions with a time period.
Answer them with at least: one filtered and sorted query, one GROUP BY with HAVING, one JOIN (with a fan-out check), one CTE and one window function.
Document your checks for each answer: row counts, reconciliation to a total, and two spot-checked rows.
Write plain-language findings with one or two charts and a note on data limits.
Publish the .sql files and README on GitHub or a shared document, and write your 90-day plan naming one target opportunity and monthly measurable actions.
